title: Episode 96: Reddit Trending — The dietary fibre content of fruit and vegetable kitchen preparation waste and UK consumers’ dietary fibre-related attitudes regarding its consumption

description:
**Top Trending Friday** — our weekly pick of the top-trending paper on r/science this week.

**[The dietary fibre content of fruit and vegetable kitchen preparation waste and UK consumers' dietary fibre-related attitudes regarding its consumption](https://doi.org/10.1080/09637486.2026.2734852)**

*International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, 2026*

DOI: [10.1080/09637486.2026.2734852](https://doi.org/10.1080/09637486.2026.2734852)

**Question:** Do discarded peels, stalks, cores and seeds of 12 fruits and vegetables hold more fibre than the parts we eat, and would consumers eat them?

**Answer:** Trimmings measured 2.10 to 9.26 g fibre/100 g and beat database flesh values in 10 of 12, but from one specimen each against an unpaired reference. Forty campus focus-group participants preferred a health pitch to a sustainability one.

**Three takeaways**

1. Trimmings were fibre-richer in 10 of 12 (pineapple 6.64 vs 1.2 g/100 g), mostly insoluble; broccoli stalk and fennel core were lower.
2. One specimen per item versus database flesh values: kale's +6.6% is a tie, and its fibre fractions don't sum.
3. Participants favoured health messaging and dishes that feel like normal food, but knew the study's aims.

source_metadata.journal: International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition
source_metadata.abstract: "Root-to-tip" eating, which incorporates typically discarded edible plant components such as peels, skins, seeds and stalks into cooking, may reduce food waste while increasing dietary fibre intake. Although fruit and vegetable by-products have been explored to enhance fibre content in foods, the fibre content of many "root-to-tip" components remains unknown. This study quantified total dietary fibre (TDF) in "root-to-tip" and commonly consumed components of 12 types of raw fresh produce. Focus groups with higher education foodservice consumers explored perceptions of fibre and "root-to-tip" eating to inform future interventions. TDF content of "root-to-tip" components ranged from 2.10 g/100 g (watermelon skin) to 9.25 g/100 g (butternut squash skin and seeds) and exceeded that of commonly consumed components in 10 of 12 produce types. Participants viewed nutritional benefits, particularly fibre, as a stronger motivator than sustainability. These findings suggest "root-to-tip" eating could support higher dietary fibre intake while reducing food waste.
